summaries.example: Imagine sorting a basket of toys. You could use symbols for “red toys,” “round toys,” and “red and round toys.” Combining the groups, finding what they share, or removing one group can be described with rules. Boole’s idea was to use this kind of symbol work to study whether arguments are correct.
summaries.summary: The algebra of logic is a tradition that represents logical ideas with mathematical symbols. George Boole started the modern tradition in 1847. He showed how statements about groups, or classes, could be changed into equations. Then algebraic methods could help test arguments and find conclusions. His work was powerful but had difficult features, including operations that were not always defined. William Stanley Jevons proposed a more regular system using operations such as union and intersection. Charles Sanders Peirce expanded the subject to relations and quantifiers. Ernst Schröder brought many earlier results together in a large, organized work. Later, Edward Huntington studied different axiom systems, Marshall Stone studied models of Boolean algebra, and Thoralf Skolem developed ways to remove quantifiers and decide certain questions. Alfred Tarski revived algebraic work on relations and connected it with modern logic. The tradition did not remain the only approach to logic, but it helped shape several important areas of mathematics and logic.
key_ideas: George Boole began a major tradition by turning logical statements into equations and solving them with symbolic methods.
Boole’s early system used some operations only in special cases. Jevons later favored operations that could always be used.
Charles Sanders Peirce extended the work from classes to relations, such as “is next to” or “knows.”
Ernst Schröder organized much of the nineteenth-century work, while later thinkers studied axioms, models, and decision procedures.
The tradition helped lead toward model theory and later algebraic approaches to logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows how people can turn reasoning into a system of symbols and rules. It also shows that a useful system can be improved: later thinkers made operations clearer, checked which axioms were needed, studied different models, and found procedures for deciding some logical questions. These ideas helped connect logic with algebra, relations, and model theory.

important_terms.definition: A way to use symbols and rule-like operations to study the structure of logical reasoning.
A group of objects treated together, such as all red toys or all birds.
A statement or rule that can be used to build a logical system.
A relationship in which one class is included inside another class.
A possible setting in which the rules of a logical system are true.

questions_to_think_about: How is sorting objects like working with logical classes?
Why might it be useful to replace a long list of argument examples with general rules?
What could go wrong if a symbol operation worked only sometimes?
Why would mathematicians want to study different models of the same rules?

summaries.example: Suppose A is the class of students who play chess and B is the class of students who play tennis. The intersection A∩B represents students in both classes, while A⊆B says every chess player is also a tennis player. Boole tried to represent statements of this kind as equations and use algebraic transformations to derive consequences. Peirce’s relation-based work would allow us to study a relation such as “student x tutors student y,” including its converse and composition.
summaries.summary: The algebra of logic tradition began with George Boole’s attempt to give deductive logic an algebraic form. In his 1847 work and its fuller 1854 presentation, logical claims about classes were represented by equations, and general theorems supplied procedures for analyzing many possible arguments rather than merely listing familiar syllogisms. The system was innovative but not straightforwardly ordinary arithmetic: some operations were partial, particular propositions raised semantic and algebraic problems, and Boole’s proposed foundations were not fully justified. Jevons moved toward total operations, especially unrestricted union and intersection, helping prepare the way for Boolean algebra and equational logic. Peirce replaced equality as the central primitive with subsumption, accepted empty classes, and extended the approach to binary relations. De Morgan had already analyzed relation composition and converse, while Peirce introduced operations corresponding to quantification. Schröder systematized these developments and investigated equations involving relations, though his treatment included claims that required correction or criticism. Huntington studied independent and equivalent axiom systems. Stone developed representation results showing that every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to an algebra of sets and linked Boolean algebras with Boolean rings and special topological spaces. Löwenheim and Skolem connected the tradition with model theory and quantifier elimination. Tarski later revived relation algebra and developed algebraic systems intended to capture important parts of first-order logic.
key_ideas: Boole’s innovation was algorithmic: translate logical information into equations, apply algebraic techniques, and translate the result back when possible.
Boole’s treatment differed from modern Boolean algebra in important ways, including partial operations and unresolved questions about foundations and existential claims.
Jevons replaced Boole’s partial addition with unrestricted union, while Peirce used subsumption as a basic relation and allowed classes to be empty.
Peirce and De Morgan developed algebraic treatments of binary relations; Peirce also used general sums and products to represent quantification.
Schröder systematized the tradition in three volumes, addressing classes, existential statements, and relations, although some of his claims and methods were challenged.
Huntington, Stone, Skolem, and Tarski shifted attention toward axioms, models, elimination procedures, decidability, and algebraic versions of first-order logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The tradition illustrates a central question about logic: should logic be viewed mainly as a calculus of symbolic operations, a universal language, or both? Its results influenced Boolean algebra, relation algebra, model theory, equational logic, and decision procedures. It also demonstrates why formal systems require more than clever notation: one must clarify meanings, prove that rules are sound, identify models, compare axiom systems, and determine the limits of what the system can express or decide.

important_terms.definition: A nineteenth-century program that expresses logical structure through algebraic operations, equations, and related formal systems.
A collection of objects treated as one unit in a logical analysis; nineteenth-century systems often reasoned about classes.
A relation meaning that one class is contained in another; it can also represent implication in some settings.
A statement accepted as a starting point for deriving other statements in an axiomatic system.
A mathematical structure in which the axioms or formulas of a system receive an interpretation and are true.
A method that transforms formulas so that quantified variables no longer appear, when such a transformation is available.
The property of having a procedure that determines whether statements in a specified theory are valid or satisfiable.
A mathematical system for studying binary relations with operations such as union, composition, converse, and complement.

questions_to_think_about: Why might equations be a better tool than a memorized catalog of valid syllogisms?
What are the advantages and risks of treating an operation as total rather than defined only in special cases?
How does allowing empty classes change the interpretation of statements such as “All A are B”?
Why is a proof that an axiom system is independent or equivalent to another system philosophically useful?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, when first-order logic is represented by an algebraic structure?

summaries.example: Think about a school club list. Let C be the students in the chess club and M the students in the music club. C∩M is the group in both clubs, and C∪M is everyone in at least one club. A statement such as “Every chess-club member is a music-club member” says C is contained in M. Boole tried to express such claims with equations. Later systems made these group operations more dependable and used them to study arguments.
summaries.summary: The algebra of logic tradition is the historical effort to represent logical reasoning with algebraic symbols. George Boole began its modern form in 1847. He treated classes as mathematical objects and translated statements about them into equations. Algebraic techniques could then be used to derive conclusions, offering a general procedure instead of a small memorized list of syllogisms. Boole’s approach was important but difficult. Some operations were allowed only for certain classes, and his account of particular statements and the foundations of the system raised questions. William Stanley Jevons proposed total operations, especially union and intersection, and helped move the subject toward Boolean algebra. Charles Sanders Peirce developed a different foundation based on subsumption and allowed classes to be empty, a move closer to modern semantics. Augustus De Morgan and Peirce also developed algebraic work on binary relations, such as relations that can be composed or reversed. Peirce used general sums and products to represent quantifiers. Ernst Schröder organized these developments in a major three-volume treatment. In the twentieth century, Huntington investigated axioms, Stone studied representations and models of Boolean algebras, and Skolem developed quantifier-elimination results for the calculus of classes. These results helped connect the tradition to model theory. Tarski later revived relation algebra and developed algebraic systems related to first-order logic.
key_ideas: Boole changed logic from mainly memorizing accepted argument forms into using general symbolic rules and procedures.
His system translated claims about classes into equations, but its partial operations and treatment of particular claims caused difficulties.
Jevons argued for total operations such as ordinary union, while Peirce developed subsumption and accepted that classes may be empty.
De Morgan and Peirce extended the subject to relations, including ways to combine and reverse relations and to represent quantifiers.
Schröder gathered and organized major nineteenth-century results, but later work showed that some proposed algebraic laws needed correction.
Later researchers studied axioms and their independence, possible models, quantifier elimination, decidability, and algebraic forms of first-order logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The story matters because it shows how logic became more mathematical and more systematic. It also shows that formal reasoning involves several tasks: choosing basic operations, explaining their meanings, proving which rules follow, finding models, and identifying what can be decided. The work of Boole, Jevons, Peirce, Schröder, Stone, Skolem, and Tarski helped shape modern logic and parts of abstract algebra.

important_terms.definition: A tradition that studies logic by representing classes, relations, and reasoning with algebraic symbols and operations.
A group considered as a single collection, such as all students in a club.
A rule or starting statement from which other results can be proved.
The relation of one class being contained in another; it can also express implication.
A mathematical interpretation in which a formal system’s rules hold.
A statement about whether at least one object exists in a class or relation.
A symbol or expression that indicates how widely a statement applies, such as “all” or “some.”

questions_to_think_about: Why might a general method be more useful than a list of examples?
Why would allowing an empty class affect the truth of a statement?
What is the difference between studying the rules of a system and studying its possible models?
Why might mathematicians want a procedure that decides questions automatically?
How can extending logic from classes to relations make it more powerful?
